nodes.ask: Pregnant or just delivered, bleeding or acutely unwell. First moves?
options: Airway, breathing, pulse, vitals; IV access, blood count, group and Rh; hCG if not known
Digital cervical exam to judge dilation, then bloods and imaging as the findings suggest
Quantitative hCG first, holding the other tests until the level is back to guide the workup next
Transvaginal ultrasound before vitals or bloods, so the site of the pregnancy is known first
nodes.chainStep: Airway, breathing, pulse and vitals; IV access; blood count, group and Rh type; pregnancy test if pregnancy is not known; establish the gestation
nodes.why: Resuscitation in pregnancy follows the usual algorithm, so check airway, breathing and pulse first. A pulse over 100 or a pressure under 100/60 is a warning sign of an ectopic. Send a blood count and the blood group with Rh type, offer a pregnancy test whenever pregnancy is possible, and set the gestation, which picks the route. After 20 weeks, check earlier scans for the placenta before any vaginal exam.

orders.dose: Determine the mother's Rh type early; anti-D after a sensitizing event is handled on each route

nodes.note: Major trauma in pregnancy belongs to the trauma pathway. A seizure or headache with hypertension hands off to the seizure and headache pathways.

nodes.label: Pulse, vitals, pregnancy test and gestation

outcomes.if: Cardiac arrest, pregnant; no pulse, fundus at or above the umbilicus
Hypertension after 20 weeks or after birth; new BP over 140/90 with a seizure, severe headache or visual change, no heavy bleeding

orders.dose: Pre-eclampsia: new hypertension over 140/90 after 20 weeks with proteinuria or other new organ dysfunction; severe headache and visual blurring or flashing are its symptoms. Eclampsia: the convulsive form

outcomes.if: Outside this pathway; pregnancy test negative, 14+0 to 19+6 weeks, arrest with the fundus below the umbilicus, or bleeding over 24 hours after birth

orders.dose: Resuscitative hysterotomy is not recommended when the fundus is below the umbilicus (under 20 weeks); standard ACLS
Bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth; its management is not covered here

outcomes.if: Early pregnancy, in shock; positive test, up to 13 weeks, hypotensive or tachycardic
Early pregnancy, stable; positive test, up to 13 weeks, pulse and BP normal
After 20 weeks, bleeding with shock; hypotensive or tachycardic
After 20 weeks, bleeding, stable; pulse and BP normal
After birth, heavy bleeding; within 24 hours of delivery

nodes.ask: Pregnant, fundus above the umbilicus, no pulse; CPR under way. Add?
options: Manual left uterine displacement; resuscitative hysterotomy if no pulse returns by 4 minutes
Tilt the board to the left side, then move her to theatre for a cesarean delivery
Withhold defibrillation and epinephrine to protect the fetus, and wait for obstetrics to arrive
Keep up standard CPR and leave delivery of the baby until the arrest is over
nodes.chainStep: CPR flat on her back with manual left uterine displacement; ACLS unchanged, defibrillation included; resuscitative hysterotomy where she lies if no pulse by 4 minutes, delivery within 5
nodes.why: Above the umbilicus the uterus compresses the vena cava and aorta. Push it to the left by hand and keep her flat: tilting the board weakens compressions. Airway, compressions, drugs and defibrillation are the same as outside pregnancy. From 20 weeks, if circulation has not returned within 4 minutes, start a resuscitative hysterotomy where she lies, aiming to deliver within 5 minutes; moving her to theatre loses that time, and it is still worth doing after 5 minutes. With a non-shockable rhythm or an unwitnessed arrest, FEBRASGO starts it as soon as possible.

sources.where: Key points; Manual uterine displacement; Resuscitative hysterotomy

orders.dose: One or both hands on the right side of the uterus, pushing it to the left; do not tilt the table
From 20 weeks with no return of circulation by 4 minutes: start at the site of collapse, deliver within 5 minutes; still perform it if 5 minutes have passed
Airway management, CPR and defibrillation as in a woman who is not pregnant
Call them in when the fetus may be viable, beyond 22 to 24 weeks

nodes.ask: Positive test in early pregnancy, in shock. Next?
options: Resuscitate, call gynecology now, and find the source: bedside ultrasound and a speculum exam
Two serum hCG levels 48 hours apart, then a transvaginal scan once the pattern of change is clear
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast to find where the bleeding is coming from
Methotrexate now, before the result of a scan, to stop a likely ectopic from growing
nodes.chainStep: Resuscitate; gynecology now; bedside ultrasound for free fluid and a speculum exam for tissue in the os; blood count, group and Rh type for transfusion
nodes.why: Instability changes the order. NICE sends the unstable woman straight to the emergency department, and her hemodynamic state sets the management of a suspected ectopic. Free fluid on the scan can be hemoperitoneum; the speculum shows an open os or tissue in the canal. hCG levels and CT only delay treatment, and methotrexate is contraindicated when she is unstable.

sources.where: History and Physical; Evaluation, additional studies

outcomes.if: Suspected ruptured ectopic; free fluid, no intrauterine pregnancy, os closed
Bleeding miscarriage or cervical shock; os open, tissue in the canal, no free fluid
Source not found; no free fluid, no tissue in the os

nodes.ask: Positive test, free fluid, empty uterus, still hypotensive. Next?
options: Emergency surgery now: laparoscopy, or laparotomy if her condition demands it
Methotrexate, then serial hCG on days 4 and 7 to confirm the treatment has worked
Formal transvaginal scan and repeat hCG in 48 hours before a decision on surgery
CT angiography first, to find the bleeding vessel for embolization by radiology
nodes.chainStep: Emergency surgery, laparoscopic where her condition allows; salpingectomy for a ruptured tube; resuscitation and blood continue; no methotrexate
nodes.why: Signs of a ruptured ectopic mean urgent surgery. NICE asks for laparoscopy whenever possible, taking her condition into account. Hemodynamic instability and rupture are absolute contraindications to methotrexate, and waiting for hCG or imaging only adds blood loss. With a ruptured tube, salpingectomy is the preferred operation.

orders.dose: Avoid: hemodynamic instability and a ruptured ectopic are absolute contraindications
Preferred with rupture or major tubal damage; NICE offers it unless she has other risk factors for infertility
The sources disagree; see the note. This pathway does not key an answer on it
orders.note: NICE NG126 (June 2026): no anti-D up to 11+6 weeks for an ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage or threatened miscarriage, even with surgery; at 12+0 to 12+6 weeks, offer at least 250 IU (50 micrograms) with medical or surgical management, and consider it for threatened miscarriage with heavy or recurrent bleeding. FIGO 2021: 500 IU (100 micrograms) after an ectopic pregnancy at any gestation or a surgical abortion, and after a spontaneous or medical miscarriage beyond 10 weeks. US: the RhoGAM label covers actual or threatened pregnancy loss at any stage and ectopic pregnancy (300 micrograms up to and including 12 weeks), and StatPearls gives it after any surgical uterine evacuation; StatPearls: 50 to 120 micrograms IM in the first trimester, 300 after 12 weeks.

nodes.ask: Os open, tissue in the canal, hypotensive. Next?
options: Remove the tissue from the os at the bedside, then emergency uterine evacuation
Misoprostol 800 micrograms and expectant care while the fluids run in
Fluids and vasopressors, leaving the tissue in place until she reaches theatre for evacuation
Mifepristone, then misoprostol 48 hours later, once she has been stabilized
nodes.chainStep: Remove products of conception from the cervical os at the bedside; resuscitate; emergency uterine evacuation (aspiration or suction curettage)
nodes.why: Hemorrhage and instability rule out expectant and medical care: she needs the uterus emptied as an emergency. Tissue lodged in the cervical canal can cause cervical shock, a vagal fall in pressure and pulse that fluids do not correct and that settles once the tissue is taken out at the bedside.

orders.dose: Aspiration or suction curettage; NICE offers manual vacuum aspiration under local anaesthetic or surgery in theatre
Doxycycline 200 mg 1 hour before uterine evacuation; the route differs between sources
orders.note: StatPearls Early Pregnancy Loss gives it orally; StatPearls Incomplete Miscarriage gives it intravenously.

nodes.ask: Positive test, early pregnancy, stable. Next?
options: Transvaginal ultrasound for location and heartbeat, with a speculum exam
A single quantitative hCG to decide whether the pregnancy is in the uterus
Methotrexate today if the hCG is above the discriminatory level, without a scan
CT of the abdomen and pelvis to look for an ectopic pregnancy
nodes.chainStep: Transvaginal ultrasound to locate the pregnancy and look for a fetal pole and heartbeat; speculum exam for the os and tissue
nodes.why: A transvaginal scan shows where the pregnancy is and whether there is a heartbeat; a serum hCG cannot locate it. Methotrexate on a first visit needs a definite ectopic with a viable intrauterine pregnancy excluded. The speculum exam shows whether the os is open and tissue is passing.

outcomes.if: Viable intrauterine pregnancy; heartbeat seen, os closed
Viability uncertain; no heartbeat yet, embryo under 7 mm or sac under 25 mm with no embryo

orders.dose: US: repeat in 7 to 10 days. NICE: a second scan at least 7 days after the first before any diagnosis; a 24-hour contact number meanwhile

sources.where: Evaluation, early intrauterine pregnancies of unknown viability

outcomes.if: Missed miscarriage; no heartbeat at 7 mm or more, or an empty sac of 25 mm or more, confirmed, os closed

orders.dose: US criteria: an embryo of 7 mm or more without a heartbeat, or a sac of 25 mm or more without an embryo, is diagnostic; NICE asks for a second opinion or a second scan at least 7 days later first

sources.where: Evaluation, findings consistent with pregnancy failure

outcomes.if: Incomplete or inevitable miscarriage; os open, tissue in the uterus or canal, no fever
Septic miscarriage; fever, uterine tenderness, offensive discharge
Complete miscarriage; uterus empty, os closed, an earlier scan showed an intrauterine pregnancy

orders.dose: Home urine pregnancy test 3 weeks after the miscarriage; return if positive (NICE states it after expectant management). Without an earlier scan confirming an intrauterine pregnancy, treat it as a pregnancy of unknown location

outcomes.if: Molar pregnancy suspected; cystic placenta, no fetal parts, hCG far above dates
No intrauterine pregnancy; an adnexal mass, or nothing seen

nodes.ask: Heartbeat seen, os closed, light bleeding. Plan?
options: Expectant care; review if bleeding worsens; progesterone only after a past miscarriage
Strict bed rest at home and pelvic rest until the bleeding has stopped completely, then a repeat scan
Misoprostol to complete what is likely to become a miscarriage
Uterine aspiration to prevent a later, heavier miscarriage
nodes.chainStep: Expectant care: return if bleeding worsens or lasts beyond 14 days; vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily if she has miscarried before; no bed rest
nodes.why: A viable intrauterine pregnancy with a closed os is managed expectantly. NICE asks her to return if the bleeding worsens or lasts beyond 14 days, and offers vaginal progesterone only to women who have miscarried before. Bed rest does not prevent miscarriage. Misoprostol and aspiration would end a viable pregnancy.

orders.dose: Vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily; continue to 16 completed weeks once a heartbeat is confirmed
The sources disagree; see the note. This pathway does not key an answer on it

nodes.ask: Confirmed missed miscarriage, stable, no infection. Options?
options: Expectant care, mifepristone then misoprostol, or uterine aspiration, after discussing each
Oxytocin infusion on the ward to make the uterus expel the pregnancy, and surgery if that fails overnight
Repeat hCG in 48 hours to confirm the pregnancy has failed
Admit for daily hCG until the level halves, then choose treatment
nodes.chainStep: Discuss expectant care (NICE first line, 7 to 14 days), mifepristone 200 mg by mouth then misoprostol 800 micrograms 24 (US) or 48 (NICE) hours later, or uterine aspiration
nodes.why: All three work when she is stable and not infected. US practice lets her preference choose; NICE starts with 7 to 14 days of expectant care unless, for example, she is at higher risk from bleeding or shows signs of infection, and offers medication if waiting is not acceptable. Mifepristone before misoprostol succeeds more often than misoprostol alone. Serial hCG belongs to a pregnancy of unknown location, not to a miscarriage the scan has confirmed. Oxytocin is not one of the options: its label calls curettage the primary therapy in the first trimester.

orders.dose: Mifepristone 200 mg by mouth, then 48 hours later misoprostol 800 micrograms vaginal, oral or sublingual
orders.note: The US regimen waits 24 hours; see the next order.

orders.dose: Mifepristone 200 mg by mouth, then 24 hours later misoprostol 800 micrograms vaginally; misoprostol may be repeated once, 3 hours to 7 days later
Manual vacuum aspiration under local anaesthetic, or surgery in theatre
Home urine pregnancy test 3 weeks later

nodes.ask: Os open, tissue in the uterus, stable, no infection. Options?
options: Expectant care, misoprostol, or uterine aspiration, after discussing each
Mifepristone by mouth, then misoprostol 48 hours later, as for a missed miscarriage
Repeat the scan in 7 to 10 days, then offer treatment
Antibiotics for 7 days, then a repeat scan
nodes.chainStep: Discuss expectant care, misoprostol alone (NICE 600 micrograms once, vaginal, oral or sublingual; US 800 vaginally) or uterine aspiration; no mifepristone for an incomplete miscarriage
nodes.why: Expectant, medical and surgical care all work for an incomplete or inevitable miscarriage, and waiting does well when tissue is already passing. NICE uses misoprostol alone, 600 micrograms once (800 as an alternative), and does not offer mifepristone here. A repeat scan in 7 to 10 days is for uncertain viability, not a miscarriage already under way, and antibiotics are not indicated unless there is an infection.

orders.dose: 600 micrograms once, vaginal, oral or sublingual; 800 micrograms as an alternative
US: 800 micrograms vaginally, a second dose 3 hours to 7 days later if needed. WHO: 400 micrograms sublingually or 600 micrograms orally once, under 14 weeks
Not for an incomplete miscarriage
Hemodynamic instability, high risk of hemorrhage, sepsis, or failed expectant or medical care

nodes.ask: Cystic placenta, no fetal parts, hCG far above dates. Treatment?
options: Suction evacuation under ultrasound guidance, then serial hCG until normal
Misoprostol to induce passage of the mole at home, then a scan in 2 weeks to confirm it has gone
Methotrexate first, with evacuation later if the hCG plateaus
Hysterotomy to remove the mole intact for histology
nodes.chainStep: Suction evacuation and curettage under ultrasound guidance, oxytocin infusion from the start of suction, histology; anti-D if RhD-negative; hCG every 1 to 2 weeks
nodes.why: Suction evacuation, ideally under ultrasound guidance, is the preferred method whatever the uterine size when she wants to keep her fertility, and histology makes the diagnosis. Medical induction and hysterotomy raise morbidity and the risk of persistent disease needing chemotherapy. Prophylactic chemotherapy is kept for special situations, such as when hCG follow-up is not possible.

sources.where: Clinical presentation, molar pregnancy; Treatment, molar pregnancy

orders.dose: An IV infusion may start at the onset of suction and continue for several hours
Available when the uterus is larger than 16 weeks' size
Rh immune globulin for RhD-negative women at evacuation
Every 1 to 2 weeks; partial mole: one more normal level 1 month after it normalizes; complete mole: monthly for 6 months after it normalizes
Oral contraceptives are safe during follow-up
An alternative to suction if her family is complete

nodes.ask: Bleeding after 20 weeks, stable. Before any digital exam?
options: Placental site from earlier scans or ultrasound; continuous fetal monitoring
Digital cervical exam to check dilation and the presenting part
Kleihauer-Betke test first, to show whether the blood is fetal
Speculum and digital exam together first, then ultrasound if the os is closed
nodes.chainStep: Earlier scans and ultrasound for the placental site (transabdominal, then transvaginal if previa is suspected); continuous fetal monitoring; speculum exam; no digital exam until previa is excluded
nodes.why: Find the placenta before any digital exam, which can provoke massive bleeding from a previa. Check earlier scans, scan transabdominally and then transvaginally if previa is suspected (the transvaginal scan is safe), and start continuous fetal monitoring. A speculum exam is safe. The Kleihauer-Betke test measures fetal blood in her circulation and does not diagnose an abruption; ultrasound cannot exclude one either. In labour, check earlier scans first: with a known fundal placenta no scan is needed, and imaging never delays delivery once the tracing shows bradycardia.
nodes.note: NICE NG121 states this order for bleeding in labour; StatPearls states it for any bleeding in the second or third trimester.

Abruption, mother and fetus stable; tender uterus, placenta clear of the os, preterm

Conservative care is limited to a mild abruption before 37 weeks, so at term plan delivery
300 micrograms (1,500 IU) IM within 72 hours; extra doses sized by a test for a large bleed

Clotting studies with fibrinogen, type and crossmatch

nodes.ask: After 20 weeks: shock, heavy ongoing bleeding, or a viable fetus in distress. Next?
options: Emergency cesarean now: category 1, within 30 minutes of the decision
Formal ultrasound to confirm the cause before deciding on the route of birth
Corticosteroids and observation on the ward for 48 hours, delivering if the bleeding carries on after that
Oxytocin to speed labor and aim for a vaginal birth within the next few hours
nodes.chainStep: Emergency cesarean (category 1, within 30 minutes of the decision); with maternal bleeding or shock, two large-bore IVs, crossmatch, clotting studies and the major hemorrhage protocol; neonatal team
nodes.why: Shock, heavy or continuing bleeding, or a failing fetal heart after 20 weeks means delivery now. NICE lists suspected uterine rupture, major abruption and persistent fetal bradycardia as category 1, done within 30 minutes. A previa with excessive or continuous bleeding is delivered by cesarean whatever the gestation, imaging delays the laparotomy a rupture needs, and a torn vasa previa bleeds the fetus's own blood. The oxytocin label rules it out with total previa or vasa previa and advises against it with a scarred uterus.

orders.dose: Two large-bore IVs, blood count, crossmatch, clotting studies; trigger the major haemorrhage protocol
A unit with on-site blood transfusion
Midline incision when intraperitoneal bleeding is suspected; repair a small tear; hysterectomy for instability or major injury
General anesthesia is usually needed; neuraxial is contraindicated with hemodynamic instability
Present at the birth and told about the bleed, as the baby may be anemic

orders.dose: Stopping it is not stated in this pathway's sources
300 micrograms (1,500 IU) IM within 72 hours; extra doses sized by a test for a large bleed

nodes.ask: Placenta previa, preterm, bleeding settled, mother and fetus well. Plan?
options: Admit, corticosteroids, cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks or sooner if bleeding is heavy
Induction of labor at 37 weeks, with a cesarean if the labor stalls
Cesarean today at this gestation, before the next bleed comes
Discharge home today with no restrictions, and a routine growth scan and clinic visit at 36 weeks
nodes.chainStep: Admit; corticosteroids if preterm birth may be needed; planned cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks; cesarean at any gestation for heavy or continuing bleeding
nodes.why: A previa is delivered by cesarean; labor is ruled out with a complete previa. When the bleeding settles before 36 weeks, expectant care in hospital is reasonable, with corticosteroids for the baby's lungs and magnesium for neuroprotection if preterm birth becomes imminent, and the cesarean is planned for 36 to 37 weeks. Excessive or continuing bleeding means cesarean whatever the gestation. Discharge is considered once she has gone 48 hours without bleeding and the fetus is well.

orders.dose: NICE: offer at 24+0 to 33+6 weeks in suspected or established preterm labour or a planned preterm birth; consider at 34+0 to 35+6. StatPearls gives them to admitted previa patients who qualify
Not stated in NICE NG25
Planned or established preterm birth within 24 hours: offer at 24+0 to 29+6 weeks, consider at 30+0 to 33+6; 4 g IV over 15 minutes, then 1 g an hour until birth or for 24 hours
Two large-bore IVs, blood count, type and screen, clotting; crossmatch 2 to 4 units if bleeding is substantial
Scan for placenta accreta spectrum
Regional anaesthesia preferred; a unit with on-site blood transfusion

nodes.ask: Tender uterus, placenta clear of the os, mother and fetus stable, preterm. Plan?
options: Admit for maternal and fetal monitoring, clotting studies and crossmatched blood
Discharge home without follow-up: a normal placenta on ultrasound has excluded an abruption
Emergency cesarean now, before the abruption extends
Kleihauer-Betke test to confirm the abruption, then decide
nodes.chainStep: Admit; continuous maternal and fetal monitoring; blood count, clotting studies with fibrinogen, type and crossmatch; deliver if mother or fetus deteriorates; corticosteroids if preterm birth becomes likely
nodes.why: Abruption is a clinical diagnosis: ultrasound cannot confirm or exclude it, and the Kleihauer-Betke test measures fetal blood in her circulation rather than diagnosing it. A mild abruption with a stable mother and fetus before 37 weeks can be managed conservatively in hospital, with blood crossmatched. Deterioration of either means delivery.

Not stated in NICE NG25

nodes.ask: RhD-negative, not sensitized, bleeding after 20 weeks. Next?

No anti-D now, because the bleeding has stopped and the placenta looks normal on the scan
Wait for the routine antenatal dose at 28 weeks

nodes.chainStep: Anti-D 300 micrograms (1,500 IU) IM within 72 hours, covering 30 mL of fetal whole blood; screen for a large fetomaternal bleed (rosette, then Kleihauer-Betke) and add doses if needed
nodes.why: Bleeding after 20 weeks is a sensitizing event in an RhD-negative woman. Give anti-D within 72 hours: 300 micrograms (1,500 IU) covers 30 mL of fetal whole blood, or 15 mL of fetal red cells. A rosette screen, then a Kleihauer-Betke test if it is positive, sizes any extra dose. Waiting for 28 weeks or for the birth leaves this bleed uncovered.

nodes.ask: Heavy bleeding soon after birth, fundus felt. First response?
options: Call for help; uterine massage, IV oxytocin, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, fluids; look for the cause

nodes.chainStep: Call for help; uterine massage; IV oxytocin; tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of birth; isotonic crystalloid; empty the bladder; examine for the cause (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin)
nodes.why: The first-response bundle runs together: uterine massage, IV oxytocin (the first-line uterotonic), tranexamic acid and isotonic crystalloid, then an examination for the cause. Tranexamic acid is 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of birth, whatever the cause, with a second gram if bleeding continues after 30 minutes; delay, even a short one, reduces its benefit, and after 3 hours WHO does not support it. Methylergonovine is not given IV routinely. If no fundus can be felt, think of inversion: uterotonics stop until it is replaced.

nodes.chainStep: Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually; no carboprost with asthma; no methylergonovine or ergometrine with hypertension or pre-eclampsia
nodes.why: NICE does not offer carboprost to women with asthma because of the risk of bronchospasm, and suggests prostaglandin E1 for postpartum hemorrhage in asthma; misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog. Hypertension and pre-eclampsia rule out methylergonovine and oxytocin with ergometrine. WHO recommends sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms when the bleeding does not respond to oxytocin.

Misoprostol 800 micrograms is the other option.

A balloon comes after uterotonics fail, and surgery after conservative measures fail.

Uterine artery embolization first, before a balloon or compression is tried
Hysterectomy straight away, before a balloon, compression sutures or embolization are tried
Another hour of oxytocin infusion before anything else
nodes.chainStep: Bimanual compression while the balloon is prepared; uterine balloon tamponade; blood products; then compression sutures, artery ligation, embolization or hysterectomy if bleeding continues
nodes.why: When uterotonics fail and retained tissue and trauma are excluded, balloon tamponade is next, with surgery and blood immediately available; bimanual compression holds the bleeding meanwhile. Embolization is for when other measures have failed, and gauze packing is not recommended. If bleeding continues, compression sutures, artery ligation, embolization or hysterectomy follow, and a hysterectomy comes sooner rather than later once those fail.

nodes.ask: Firm uterus, bright bleeding from a tear. Next?
options: Repair the tear promptly under good light and adequate anesthesia
Carboprost IM, since bleeding this heavy is likely to be atony
Uterine balloon tamponade to compress the bleeding site
Pack the vagina tightly and reassess her in 24 hours before attempting a repair
nodes.chainStep: Examine the genital tract under anesthesia if needed; repair the laceration; continue tranexamic acid and resuscitation
nodes.why: Bleeding with a firm, contracted uterus points to genital tract trauma, and lacerations are repaired, with an examination under anaesthetic if needed. A balloon is for atony once trauma and retained tissue are excluded, and a uterotonic does not close a tear. Tranexamic acid still applies whatever the cause.

nodes.ask: Placenta retained, heavy bleeding. Next?
options: Manual removal under anesthesia, with a single dose of prophylactic antibiotics
Ergometrine IM to make the uterus expel the placenta
Oxytocin injected into the umbilical vein, then wait another hour for the placenta to separate
Hysterectomy, since the placenta may be morbidly adherent
nodes.chainStep: IV access; uterotonics and tranexamic acid continue; manual removal of the placenta under anesthesia; one prophylactic antibiotic dose
nodes.why: A retained placenta with heavy bleeding comes out by hand, under anaesthetic, with routine antibiotic prophylaxis. Uterotonics are given because she is bleeding, but ergometrine is avoided while the placenta is in, as its tetanic contractions can delay delivery of the placenta. Umbilical vein oxytocin belongs to research.

orders.dose: One dose: ampicillin or a first-generation cephalosporin, or amoxicillin 1 g with clavulanic acid 200 mg IV

Avoid while the placenta is retained

nodes.ask: Uterus firm, no tear, blood not clotting, fibrinogen low. Next?
options: Blood products guided by clotting tests: red cells, plasma, and fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate
A further uterotonic, since a contracted uterus can still be the source
Uterine balloon tamponade, as for atony, before the clotting tests
Large volumes of crystalloid, holding back blood products until the hemoglobin falls below a set threshold
nodes.chainStep: Near-patient coagulation testing; red cells, plasma and platelets (1:1:1 in massive hemorrhage); cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen is under 200 mg/dL, aiming for 150 to 200; tranexamic acid
nodes.why: A firm uterus with no tear and blood that will not clot is coagulopathy, after abruption, fetal death, severe pre-eclampsia or HELLP, or amniotic fluid embolism. Replace what is missing, guided by clotting tests: in massive hemorrhage, red cells, plasma and platelets 1:1:1, and fibrinogen, the first factor to fall, mostly as cryoprecipitate. Large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors further.

10 units raise fibrinogen by about 100 mg/dL; further doses by the level

nodes.ask: No fundus felt, a smooth mass in the vagina, heavy bleeding. First?
options: Hold uterotonics and push the fundus back up at once, leaving an attached placenta in place
Peel the attached placenta off first so the uterus is smaller, then replace the uterus by hand
Carboprost IM to contract the uterus before replacing it
Give oxytocin first, then replace the uterus once it has firmed
nodes.chainStep: Call for help; hold or stop uterotonics; two large-bore IVs and blood; tranexamic acid; immediate manual replacement with the placenta left attached; uterotonics once it is back; tocolytic, then surgery, if it will not go back
nodes.why: An inverted uterus is replaced by hand at once, with steady pressure on the fundus along the vaginal axis. Uterotonics stop until it is back, then restart to hold it there. Removing an attached placenta first worsens the bleeding. If replacement fails, a tocolytic relaxes the uterus, and failing that, surgery.

nodes.summary: Maternal cardiac arrest with the fundus at or above the umbilicus: CPR flat with manual left uterine displacement, ACLS unchanged, and a resuscitative hysterotomy where she lies if circulation has not returned by 4 minutes, delivering within 5. The neonatal team comes when the fetus may be viable.

Hypertension after 20 weeks or after birth with neurological symptoms: a seizure continues in the seizure pathway (eclampsia); a severe headache or visual change without a seizure continues in the headache pathway (pre-eclampsia).

Outside this pathway. Pregnancy test negative: not pregnancy bleeding. Bleeding at 14+0 to 19+6 weeks: second-trimester bleeding and loss are not in this pathway's sources yet; the early route covers up to 13 completed weeks. Arrest with the fundus below the umbilicus: standard ACLS, no resuscitative hysterotomy. Bleeding more than 24 hours after birth (secondary postpartum hemorrhage): not covered yet.
An ectopic is not excluded until the pregnancy is located; resuscitate, gynecology at the bedside, look for another source; not covered further here.
Resuscitate, start antibiotics, evacuate the uterus promptly; continue in the sepsis pathway (pw_sepsis_fever).

Bleeding settled at term: a previa from 36 weeks is delivered by cesarean; an abruption from 37 weeks is delivered rather than managed conservatively, which is for a mild abruption before 37 weeks. Anti-D within 72 hours if she is RhD-negative.
Abruption with fetal death, mother stable: deliver promptly; vaginal birth often carries less risk with coagulopathy; clotting studies, blood ready, watch for PPH. Anti-D if she is RhD-negative.

Suspected ruptured ectopic in shock: resuscitation and emergency surgery, laparoscopic where her condition allows, usually salpingectomy; never methotrexate when she is unstable. Anti-D before 13 weeks: the sources disagree.

Miscarriage with shock: remove tissue from the cervical os at the bedside (cervical shock settles once it is out), resuscitate, and evacuate the uterus as an emergency; hemorrhage rules out expectant and medical care.

Threatened miscarriage, viable intrauterine pregnancy with a closed os: expectant care, return if the bleeding worsens or lasts beyond 14 days, vaginal progesterone only after a previous miscarriage, no bed rest. Anti-D before 13 weeks: the sources disagree.
Intrauterine pregnancy of uncertain viability: one scan cannot diagnose a miscarriage. Rescan in 7 to 10 days (US) or at least 7 days later (NICE), with a 24-hour contact number meanwhile.

Missed miscarriage: expectant care, mifepristone then misoprostol (NICE 48 hours apart, US 24), or uterine aspiration, after discussion (NICE starts with 7 to 14 days of expectant care); oxytocin is not a first-trimester option; a home pregnancy test 3 weeks after medical care.

Incomplete or inevitable miscarriage, stable: expectant care, misoprostol alone (NICE 600 micrograms once; US 800 vaginally) or uterine aspiration; no mifepristone. Surgery if she becomes unstable, bleeds heavily or is infected.

Complete miscarriage after a scan had shown an intrauterine pregnancy: no further treatment and a home pregnancy test 3 weeks later. Without that earlier scan, treat it as a pregnancy of unknown location and follow hCG.

Suspected molar pregnancy: suction evacuation under ultrasound guidance with histology, anti-D if RhD-negative, then hCG every 1 to 2 weeks to normal and for a set time after (partial mole 1 month, complete mole 6 months); no medical induction or hysterotomy.

Stable, positive test, no intrauterine pregnancy (an adnexal mass, or nothing seen): continue in the abdominal pain pathway's ectopic route, where hCG, mass size, heartbeat and pain choose methotrexate, a choice of methotrexate or surgery, or surgery; a pregnancy of unknown location gets two hCG levels 48 hours apart.

Bleeding after 20 weeks with shock, heavy continuing bleeding or fetal compromise: emergency (category 1) cesarean within 30 minutes, with blood and the hemorrhage protocol when the mother is bleeding or in shock. Previa bleeding heavily: deliver whatever the gestation. Suspected uterine rupture: laparotomy, repair or hysterectomy. Vasa previa: the blood lost is the fetus's. Anti-D afterwards if she is RhD-negative.

Stable bleeding after 20 weeks, RhD-negative: anti-D within 72 hours, 300 micrograms covering 30 mL of fetal whole blood, with extra doses sized by a Kleihauer-Betke test. Previa: admit, corticosteroids if preterm, cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks or sooner for heavy bleeding. Abruption: admit, monitor mother and fetus, clotting studies, deliver if either deteriorates. No cause found: the bleed still needs anti-D.

Stable bleeding after 20 weeks, RhD-positive, so no anti-D. Previa: admit, corticosteroids if preterm, cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks or sooner for heavy bleeding. Abruption: admit, monitor mother and fetus, clotting studies, deliver if either deteriorates. No cause found: often none is identified, and this pathway's sources give no further plan.

Uterine atony: massage, IV oxytocin and tranexamic acid; if it keeps bleeding, a second uterotonic chosen by her history (carboprost when she is hypertensive, methylergonovine when her pressure is normal, misoprostol when she is hypertensive and asthmatic, carboprost avoided in asthma); if it still bleeds, bimanual compression and balloon tamponade, then compression sutures, artery ligation, embolization or hysterectomy.

Genital tract trauma, bleeding with a firm uterus: find and repair the tear under good light and anesthesia, with tranexamic acid and resuscitation continuing; a balloon or another uterotonic does not close a laceration.

Retained placenta with hemorrhage: the first-response bundle, then manual removal under anesthesia with one prophylactic antibiotic dose; no ergometrine while the placenta is in, and umbilical vein oxytocin only in research.

Coagulopathy, blood that will not clot with a firm uterus and no tear: blood products guided by clotting tests, 1:1:1 in massive hemorrhage, fibrinogen replaced when under 200 mg/dL, and small crystalloid volumes.
Uterine inversion: stop uterotonics, replace the fundus by hand at once with the placenta left attached, then restart uterotonics; a tocolytic if it will not go back, and surgery if that fails.
